This workshop aims to introduce several technical skills involved in modern empirical data analysis – retrieving data from an online repository, working with computer code in a reproducible fashion, version-controlling your analysis and publishing a reproducible report – through an applied "replication" exercise.

 Participants will reproduce one of the reanalyses that were part of the Multi100 project, whose results were recently published in Nature (Aczel et al. 2026), and test the robustness of a published claim by the original author (OA) [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] – using the same data, tools, and workflow the Multi100 project used.

## What you will do

The day centres on the EU-frames case, OA's 2016 study of EU attitudes across 27 countries. You step into the role of a sixth analyst reanalysing a published claim, and you work through the same moves a researcher actually makes:

1. **Reproduce a published analyst's result.** Take the analysis code as it was submitted to the Multi100 project, run it on the original data, and land the exact coefficient it produced.
2. **Hear how a real error entered real submitted code.** Your run reproduces the recorded value first time; a second number in the public trail does not match it, and its story – a wave file read twice, caught and corrected in the open – is told with the full OSF trail on screen.
3. **State an estimand and build a DAG.** Say precisely what the study is trying to measure, then draw the causal graph that tells you which variables to adjust for.
4. **Preregister one specification, the way researchers do on OSF.** Pick one defensible analysis from a menu of choices and write down what you expect, in a shortened version of a real preregistration template, before you run anything.
5. **Run it and watch the class multiverse grow.** Submit your result and see it land on a live chart, next to your classmates' and the five published analysts'.
6. **Learn to read a specification curve.** Understand what a thousand-plus results together can, and cannot, tell you.

The exercise is a miniature version of Multi100 itself: same claim, many analysts, explicit choices, comparable results.

## Two working routes – pick the one that fits your setup

Both routes cover every task, and both reach exactly the same numbers. Whichever you choose, you do the same analysis; nobody misses anything by picking one over the other.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Route 1 – R and Positron (recommended)

Install R and the Positron editor once, before the day, then download a ready-made workspace – a single zip file holding the analysis code, the data, and a report to fill in. There is nothing to configure and no account to create: you open the folder and start working. This is the closest to how the analysis is really done, and the workspace is yours to keep afterwards.

The [Setup](setup.qmd) page walks you through the installation in plain steps. Give yourself a little time before the day, depending on what you already have.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
### Route 2 – Browser lab (nothing to install)

Open the [Browser lab](exercise/browser-lab.qmd) page and everything runs inside the tab, on a version of R that lives in your web browser. Nothing to install, no account, and it works on a borrowed or locked-down machine. The page takes ten to thirty seconds to wake up the first time; read the task while it warms. Every required task is here, at full parity with Route 1.
:::

You need no git, no GitHub account, no OSF account and no sign-ups for either route. If you would like to add version control and publishing to your toolkit later, the optional [Git and GitHub companion module](companion/git-github.qmd) shows you how, at your own pace.

## Session schedule

The day runs as four 90-minute blocks, with a 15-minute break after Block 1, a 45-minute lunch after Block 2, and a further 15-minute break after Block 3. Times below are block-relative; a facilitator maps them onto the clock on the day.

| Block | Relative time | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Block 1 – "One paper, three verdicts" | 0:00–1:30 | The three Rs (reproducibility, robustness, replicability) and the EU-frames case, ending with a first hands-on run of the constrained model. |
| Break | 1:30–1:45 | 15-minute break. |
| Block 2 – "The record's second number, then the question underneath" | 1:45–3:15 | The story of the −3.853/−3.804 gap – a wave file read twice, caught and corrected in the open – then estimands and DAGs. |
| Lunch | 3:15–4:00 | 45-minute lunch. |
| Block 3 – "Preregister like an analyst" | 4:00–5:30 | Completing a causal graph, choosing one analytical deviation from a specification menu, preregistering it, then running and submitting your own result. |
| Break | 5:30–5:45 | 15-minute break. |
| Block 4 – "Reading the multiverse" | 5:45–7:15 | Reading the class's results against the full specification curve and the five published analysts, with an introduction to inference across a multiverse of results. |
